$comment: Single source of truth for Alloy Coil's externally-controllable parameters.
Ranges, defaults and curves are taken verbatim from upstream's
FeedbackSynthControls::registerParams() so the module behaves as Synthux
voiced it. The one deliberate departure is echo time: upstream allows 5 s,
but the RP2350 build caps the buffer at COIL_ECHO_MAX_S seconds, and a
control that promises more range than the buffer can deliver would just
silently clamp.
Generated consumers (run `make params MODULE=alloycoil` after editing, and
commit the output so a normal build never needs Python):
include/param_manifest.generated.h  — C++ descriptor table
include/param_struct.generated.h    — CoilParamGoals, one instance's worth
include/param_globals.generated.h   — the firmware's one instance
../../web-configurator/src/lib/paramMapAlloyCoil.ts
`default` therefore lands in one place and reaches all four consumers of
it: the boot value of every instance (via param_struct), factory reset (via
applyParamDefaults), the VCV knob's boot position (via toPos()) and the
web slider. Changing a default here needs no C++ edit anywhere.
Targets are members of gCoilParams rather than bare globals. The board has
one engine and one set of parameters; VCV can have any number of Alloy
Coils in a rack, and while they shared one set the second module to run in
a block overwrote the first one's knobs. The struct is what lets a host own
as many independent copies as it has instances — see the note on
fillCoilParams() in include/io/IOBridge.h.
CC numbers are chosen to line up with AlloyFlux where the meaning matches
(7 volume, 91 reverb mix, 93 echo send, 95 echo mix-ish, 74/75 filters) so
a generic MIDI controller feels familiar across both modules.

params.name: pitch
params.label: String Pitch
params.doc: Resonator pitch, as a MIDI note number

params.name: fbgain
params.label: Feedback Gain
params.doc: Feedback loop gain — the main control over how much the string rings
$comment: Upstream's min is -60 dB. Narrowed to -30, deliberately keeping the
taper LINEAR — a skew was tried here and reverted, so this fixes the
dead travel without touching the feel that was preferred.
-30 dB is a loop gain of 0.032: the resonator still decays instantly,
so nothing audible is lost at the quiet end. What changes is where the
loop starts ringing — about -15 dB, which sat at 70% of travel and now
sits at 40%.
If the very quiet end turns out to matter, put min back to -60.

params.name: excite
params.label: Exciter Level
params.doc: Level of the external exciter input into the resonator
$comment_display: Stored as the multiplier the engine wants, shown as dB. 0-2 with the
default at 1.0 reads as 'already half up' to anyone who has met a
fader; the same control in dB is -inf...+6 with unity at 0, and the
neutral point names itself. Nothing on the wire changes — see
$comment: Gain on the FM/EXCITER jack before it enters the loop. SHIFT + BODY on
the panel — the top row's only shift-secondary, pinned to the knob
position rather than to whichever parameter sits there. It sat under
FB GAIN until BODY and FB GAIN traded places; see Pot::EXCITE in
io/PanelMap.h for what that swap cost and why it was taken anyway.
CC 19 continues the module-specific 16/17/18 block. The AlloyFlux-
parallel choice would have been 92, which is COLOR there and is
literally the FM IN attenuverter — but Alloy Coil already spent 92 on
reverb decay, and CC numbers are one namespace across both modules.
Max 2.0, not 1.0. The jack is +/-8 V, so a Eurorack source at +/-5 V
normalises to 0.625 and unity here would put full-scale excitation out
of reach of most patches. Default 1.0 means the jack's full swing maps
to the engine's full scale, which is what it did before this existed.
skew 2 for the same reason as vol and echosend: a linear input gain
spends its top half on 6 dB and leaves nothing usable down where you
are just tickling the string.

params.name: fbbody
params.label: Body
params.doc: Resonator body size — the delay length of the feedback loop
$comment_display: Stored in seconds because that is what the engine wants; shown in
milliseconds because that is what a 1-100 ms comb is called, and it
is how the panel and the manual's knob table already describe it.
A pure x1000 rescale, so it is affine in travel: the same knob
position maps to the same value and the CC on the wire is byte for
byte identical. `skew` is inherited, not restated, so the square-law
taper is shared by both parameterisations rather than duplicated.
$comment: Square-law, which is exactly upstream's Mapping::EXP — daisysp's
fmap() computes min + t^2 * (max-min) for EXP, and skew 2.0 on a
linear range is the same expression.
This was 'log' and that was not a decision, it was the curve that
came out of translating the manifest. It matters more than it looks:
this delay length is the feedback comb, so the knob's midpoint IS a
resonant frequency. Log put it at 10 ms / 100 Hz; upstream puts it at
25.8 ms / 38.8 Hz, an octave and a third lower. The endpoints agree,
so nothing became unreachable — but the whole middle of the knob
landed somewhere else, and the middle of this knob is where the
instrument lives.
Log is arguably the better-behaved curve in the abstract, and it is a
one-word revert if the even spread in frequency turns out to be
preferred over matching Audrey II.

params.name: fblpf
params.label: Feedback LPF
params.doc: Low-pass filter in the feedback loop; tames the top end as it rings

params.name: fbhpf
params.label: Feedback HPF
params.doc: High-pass filter in the feedback loop; removes rumble from the tail

params.name: echosend
params.label: Send
params.doc: How much of the resonator is sent into the echo
$comment: Audio taper, same reasoning as vol: this is a send level and linear
leaves no useful resolution in the subtle range. skew 2 puts -20 dB
at 30% of travel instead of 10%. Matches upstream's Mapping::EXP.

params.name: echotime
params.label: Time
$comment: Square-law, matching upstream's Mapping::EXP — see fbbody above for
why skew 2.0 on a linear range is the same thing.
Also a translation artefact rather than a decision, and the drift was
large: at the knob's midpoint log gave 0.45 s against upstream's
1.29 s, and at 75% 1.34 s against 2.83 s. Nearly the whole usable
range of long echoes had been pushed into the last few percent of
travel.
The max staying at COIL_ECHO_MAX_S rather than upstream's 5 s is a
separate and deliberate departure — see the file header.

params.name: echofb
params.label: Feedback
params.doc: Echo feedback; above unity it blooms into the soft-clip ceiling
$comment: Upstream's max is 1.5. Trimmed to 1.2 because everything above unity
blooms to the SoftClip ceiling and sounds much the same — only the
speed of the bloom differs — so 1.5 spent the top 30% of the control
on territory that is not distinguishable by ear.
At 1.2, unity lands at 83% of travel and the decaying range below it
spreads 0..~148 repeats across the first 80%, against 0..64 before.
The swell behaviour is unchanged, it just occupies the last fifth.
Deliberately NOT skewed: the taper below unity is already even, and a
skew here would only enlarge the indistinguishable region.

params.name: warp
params.label: Warp
params.doc: Doppler warp — halves the echo time, pitching the tail up as it settles
$comment: Upstream Audrey II's one panel switch (`kDelaySwitchPin`), which scales
the echo time by 0.5. The effect is a side effect of how a delay line
works: shortening the time while the buffer is full drags the read head
toward the write head, so everything already in the line is re-read
faster and pitches up before settling at the new time.
A parameter and not just a button because the panel button is the one
control surface Alloy Coil's firmware does not have yet — no
IHardwareIO, so MIDI, SysEx and the serial console are all it has. This
row is what puts warp on the wire, in the Alloy Controller and in the
patch dump; when the panel button lands, io/IOBridge.h writes this same
global and the two agree by construction.
The scaling is applied in ControlSmoother::Step(), not in IOBridge:
that is the one point both front ends and every transport pass through
on the way to the engine, and it leaves echoTime holding the *knob's*
time, so a preset saved with warp on does not come back half as long.
Latching on the wire, momentary on the panel. A CC is a value, not a
gesture; a held button gives the dive on press and the rise on release,
which is the playable version and is what the panel does.
CC 20 continues the module-specific 16/17/18/19 block and is free in
AlloyFlux too — CC numbers are one namespace across both modules.

params.name: revdecay
params.label: Decay
$comment: This is a tank feedback coefficient, and reverb time goes as
1/ln(fb) — so it runs away near 1.0 and barely moves below 0.7.
Linear gave 0.28..2.5 s across the first 80% of travel and then
0.28 s..infinity in the last 20%.
skew 0.5 makes the decay time close to geometric instead: roughly a
1.3-1.4x step per 10% of travel, 0.28 s -> 5 s over the first 80%,
with the freeze end still at the top.
Modelled against T60 = D * ln(0.001)/ln(fb) with D ~= 65 ms, the
average of ReverbSc's eight tank loops at 48 kHz.

params.name: vol
params.label: Volume
$comment: Square-law audio taper. Linear-in-amplitude spends its whole top half
on 6 dB (0.9 dB per 10% of travel by the end) while the bottom 10%
covers -inf..-20 dB, so the fader feels dead high and twitchy low.
skew 2 evens that out to ~4.0 dB per 10% at midpoint and ~1.9 dB at
the top, and gives real resolution down at -20..-40 dB. This is what
upstream's Mapping::EXP was doing.
